title: Monitoring with pg_stat_statements
description: Identify top slow queries, track buffer cache hit ratios, and monitor lock contention with pg_stat_statements.

data.text: **`pg_stat_statements`** is the gold standard extension for tracking query performance. It normalizes query text (replacing literal arguments with `$1`, `$2`), aggregating execution frequency, cumulative duration, and I/O buffer reads across all running queries.

data.title: Finding the Top 5 Most Time-Consuming Queries
data.content: Identifies which queries consume the most CPU and I/O in aggregate.
data.code:
SELECT 
    queryid,
    substring(query, 1, 60) AS short_query,
    calls,
    round(total_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS total_time_ms,
    round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS avg_time_ms,
    round((100.0 * shared_blks_hit / nullif(shared_blks_hit + shared_blks_read, 0))::numeric, 2) AS cache_hit_pct
FROM pg_stat_statements
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 5;

data.text: Cache Hit Ratio and Lock Monitoring

`pg_stat_statements` answers what is slow, but you also need to know whether those queries are served from memory or disk, and whether they are blocked on locks. The two queries below give the buffer cache hit ratio and any sessions currently waiting.

data.title: Cache hit ratio and current waits
data.content: A hit ratio below about 99% on an OLTP workload suggests the working set does not fit in cache. The wait query shows the blocking PID so you can trace the chain.
data.code:
-- Buffer cache hit ratio
SELECT
    sum(blks_hit) * 100.0 / nullif(sum(blks_hit) + sum(blks_read), 0) AS cache_hit_ratio
FROM pg_stat_database;

-- Sessions currently waiting on a lock
SELECT
    a.pid,
    a.usename,
    a.wait_event_type,
    a.wait_event,
    pg_blocking_pids(a.pid) AS blocked_by,
    left(a.query, 60)      AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity AS a
WHERE a.wait_event_type = 'Lock';

data.title: Interview angle: measure aggregate cost, not anecdotes
data.text: A good monitoring answer does not start from a single slow query someone complained about. It starts from `pg_stat_statements` ranked by total execution time, because a query that runs in 5 ms but is called a million times costs more than a 2-second report. Then it adds the cache hit ratio, wait events, and lock chains to explain why the expensive queries are expensive. That ordering — aggregate impact first, then mechanism — is what interviewers look for.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Enable `pg_stat_statements` in `shared_preload_libraries` for all production databases.
Focus optimization efforts on queries with the highest `total_exec_time`.
Target a cache hit ratio of 99%+ on active transactional workloads.
